content.comment_body: I have a [article_no]. I believe I may have damaged my [product_name] module. I introduced 220V AC to relays Q2 and Q3 through a bridge (with fewer cables). To enable manual operation of the circuits controlled by Q2 and Q3, I bypassed the normal setup. The outcome was that manual activation led to 220V AC at both sides of the corresponding relay. After about 20 manual bypass activations, the [product_name] started showing strange input behavior and then stopped working. I suspect this is due to the above actions, but it could possibly have been a lightning strike, though my [product_name] is grounded to the house circuit. What do experienced members think happened? For my replacement [product_name], I’m considering installing diodes on the output wires for Q2 and Q3—would this be a suitable protection method? Also, does anyone know someone who can service a [product_name] module at a lower price than what is available in Athens, Greece?

To answer your question accurately, you should review your circuit diagram. Not sure what you mean by 'bite strike.' Is there any other damaged equipment in your house? Did you follow all recommended protective circuit guidelines in the manual? Please upload your plan with all necessary details. Regards, [user_name] (translated with Google)

I had a more complex setup in that module but switched to a simpler version after finding I didn’t need as much functionality. I previously shared it here—the software uses a basic "roller shutter control button UP, button DOWN" type program (see [url]). I modified it so the shader responds to temperature inputs (AI1 and AI2). I also added a temperature-controlled pump, which works well (Q1). To summarize the complex features: The setup is supposed to use three sensors associated with shader positions, so when I1, I2, or I3 activate you only trigger general program parts, not specific ones. I had to ensure at certain temperature ranges, specific inputs (I1, I2, I3) correspond to Q2 or Q3 operation, or none. Currently, only Q2 is triggered due to missing sensors (contractor issues). Bypass is used for this. Logged data never exceeded 58°C, so no conflicts there. I4 to I8 are set for reset because Q2 and Q3 shouldn’t be on simultaneously. I don’t want automatic shader activation during manual bypass (see above post). I plan to remove pump emergency activation and possibly auto activation due to external bypass since the [product_name] is so reliable. Everything—except blinds and fan—is powered by the same [product_name] power supply, including the pump. I7 acts as a shift register; I created screens for this. Mathematical functions address uneven temperature readings across the system for display uniformity. For malfunctions (e.g., PT1000 sensor), I implemented initialization and cutoff logic for shader positioning after a reset. Further down is data logging and screen color settings. Do you mean a 2A fuse between device and power supply? That's difficult to find. Cable crimping isn’t in place. Still searching for a larger, DIN, transparent, IP 64 box. I have a PC fan providing airflow from below. I did manage to install a local 220V AC 6A B-curve fuse. For the house: it's 3-phase 220V AC; at the project site, one phase uses a 220V 20A B-curve fuse. Three cables—live, neutral, ground—are arranged, and the [product_name] device uses the house's ground cable. The house infrastructure is otherwise fine. Need more details? P.S. The [product_name] simulator revealed Q2 and Q3 sometimes activated simultaneously, which shouldn't happen. I added delays to fix clock signals transmitting unexpectedly.

"Otherwise the house is fine"—so no lightning strike occurred. Your initial post mentions hardware problems and various voltages. The connection descriptions are unclear; providing a circuit diagram instead of program details is necessary for proper evaluation.

The [product_name] controller, extension module [product_name], pump, and related inputs are powered by [article_no]. There's nothing between these devices and the supply. The [product_name] controller failed (won't power on), but the extension module works with a replacement controller. Q1 draws power from [article_no] and operates the pump. Q2 and Q3 get 220V from the house. The roller blind also receives 220V from the house, with usage up to 4A (with margin). Grounding is done via the house system as needed. Manipulating the blind independently wasn’t possible without routing 220V in parallel to the [product_name], causing manual blind operation (via Q2/Q3) to place 220V at the output ends. "Auto/manual" was enabled, yet Q2 or Q3 relays were not energized even if requested. When input 4 stopped working as programmed, I used a different input. Could this relate to manually operating the blind? Later, the controller powered off permanently. Is providing 220V to Q2/Q3 output terminals the cause? Would installing a diode at Q2 and Q3 outputs to limit current be recommended? All I can do is provide a drawing.
If my previous description was unclear, here's an updated drawing for reference.

Sorry if my response seemed harsh, but no electrician can work effectively with a drawing as vague as that. With the information provided, it’s unlikely anyone here can help you. Honestly, it doesn’t seem you have sufficient expertise in this field. !! REMINDER !! 230V is hazardous and may cause severe harm. Only certified professionals should perform work on mains voltage circuits. Best regards, [user_name]
I apologize if my response was blunt, but you don’t answer direct questions and seem to focus on personal criticism. Thank you.

analysis.insight_summary: The thread discusses hardware failure likely due to incorrect wiring or manual high-voltage relay operation on a [company_name] logic device. Core topics include pinpointing the failure’s cause (misuse, voltage feedback, faulty wiring), appropriate manual relay handling, and protecting outputs safely. There is a recognized need for better documentation and clearer user understanding about correct high-voltage circuit design, safe output control, and product protection.
analysis.user_expectations: The user seeks advice on safe high-voltage circuit design for both manual and automated relay use, recommendations for hardware protection like using diodes, and suggestions for affordable repair options for damaged [company_name] modules.
